title: #54 Ask Students Not to Say or Write Anything for 30 Seconds
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton addresses the reflexive "I don't get it" response that surfaces the instant students meet an unfamiliar problem, arguing that the real obstacle is often a lack of a starting strategy rather than genuine inability. His proposed fix is to instruct students not to say or write anything for the first 30 seconds after a problem is revealed, using that pause purely for thinking. He explains the two halves of the rule separately: silence heads off the reflexive "I don't get it," while withholding writing stops students from diving in without reading the question properly, giving them time to plot a route through the problem first. Drawing on Daniel Kahneman's dual-process framework, Barton describes the 30 seconds as giving students' deliberate "System 2" a chance to override an instinctive but often faulty "System 1" reaction. He acknowledges the technique meets resistance at first -- 30 seconds can feel like three hours -- and recommends explaining the rationale to students up front so they buy into the practice once they notice its benefit, especially under exam conditions.
points: Framing the "I don't get it" reflex as an automatic System 1 reaction (via Kahneman) gives teachers a psychological rationale, not just a behavioural rule, for the 30-second pause.

The silence rule and the no-writing rule solve two distinct problems: silence blocks the verbal reflex of giving up, while withholding writing stops students from committing to the first idea before reading the question properly.
Because the technique feels uncomfortable at first, Barton recommends explicitly explaining the reasoning to students to secure buy-in rather than just imposing the rule.
The payoff Barton highlights is transferable beyond the classroom -- students who internalise the pause report benefiting from it in exam conditions.
quotes: A potential solution is asking students not to say or write anything for 30 seconds. Instead, they are to think about the problem.
We might ask students not to say anything because it prevents the reflex response of “I don’t get it” whenever students are faced with anything unfamiliar.
It prevents them from diving in head first without properly reading the question. It allows them to plot a route through the problem.
In the language of psychologist Daniel Kahneman, those 30 seconds give our students’ more thoughtful System 2s a chance to override their more instinctual, but often faulty, System 1s.

When you first introduce this approach, you are likely to be met by resistance. Those 30 seconds will feel like 3 hours, and students will be desperate to ask you questions or to write something down.
And when students start to notice the benefit of those 30 seconds of calm contemplation, especially in exams, most should jump on board.
